ann_117.original: Through this part, a capital gain above roughly 5200 US dollars pushes the model's predicted chance of earning at most 50k down faster than the direct capital-gain edge does on its own: the model reads a large gain as strong evidence of a higher income. In the typical case (a 37-year-old married man, high-school graduate, 40 hours a week, born in the United States) the hinge node 1485 is off at 5100 US dollars and on at 5200 US dollars, and reaches 0.49 at 20000 US dollars. Its second exit, node 4262, passes the hinge on to the output with a further negative weight, so both exits lower the score as the gain grows. The hinge is on for 1877 training rows, whose outcome rate is 5.8% and mean predicted chance 8%; on those rows the part adds -2.37 to the score on average, against the part's training mean. Birth in Ecuador holds the hinge off: with the Ecuador input set, node 1485 is 0 even at 99999 US dollars. This exception is fitted to few rows: 37 training rows are Ecuador-born and 1 of them has a gain above 5000 dollars. The native-country:15 input of node 4262 has 0 training rows, so its term is constant on the training data. Switching the part off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9114, because the direct capital-gain edge already ranks these rows.
ann_117.proposed: A first threshold on capital gains: gains change nothing until about 5258 US dollars, then lower the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) steadily; for a typical person born in Ecuador it is held off, so there gains lower it less, slowly at first, then faster.

ann_118.original: A second capital-gain hinge (node 262) with its own exceptions. In the typical case it switches on between 4800 US dollars and 4900 US dollars and reaches 1.22 at 20000 US dollars; through its negative output weight it lowers the predicted chance of earning at most 50k further as the gain grows. It is held off for people born in Jamaica, Nicaragua, the Philippines or Scotland, through node 2391, which fires for these four countries (374 training rows), and for people whose education level is 9th grade, through a negative weight on that level. Probe of the typical case with each of these set, at a gain of 99999 US dollars: node 262 is 0 for 9th grade, 0 for Jamaica, 0 for Nicaragua, 0 for the Philippines and 0 for Scotland, against 7.65 for the US-born case. The exceptions are fitted to few rows: 23 training rows are in one of these groups and have a capital gain above 5000 dollars. The hinge is on for 1993 training rows (outcome rate 11.7%), where it adds -2.13 to the score on average. Switching it off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9114.
ann_118.proposed: A second threshold on capital gains: gains change nothing until about 4883 US dollars, then lower the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) steadily; for a typical person born in Jamaica it is held off, so there gains lower it less, slowly at first, then faster.

ann_119.original: The model's predicted chance of earning at most 50k falls with age up to the mid-forties and rises again after that, as in a career that peaks in mid-life. The fall comes from the direct age edge (-1.03 on the score per sd of age); this part is the rise: a hinge on age (node 2990, then node 5070) whose positive weight more than cancels the direct slope once it is on. In the typical case the predicted chance falls from 92% at 17 years to 56% at 46 years; node 5070 is off at 46 years and on at 47 years (0.096), and the chance climbs back to 67% at 60.8 years and 83% at 90 years. The hinge is on for 10779 training rows, where the part adds 1.10 to the score on average. Birth in Thailand (26 training rows; node 2134 is on for 26 of them and for 26 training rows in total) sets node 2134 to 32.4, which switches the hinge on at each age in the sweep: for a Thai-born typical case the predicted chance rises with age throughout, from 71% at 17 years to 96% at 90 years. This is fitted to 26 rows. Birth in Ireland pushes node 2134 further below its threshold. Switching the part off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9023.
ann_119.proposed: Past the mid-forties, age raises the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) again: through this part, age changes nothing until about 46 years, then raises it steadily. For a typical person born in Thailand it reads age the other way, so the predicted chance rises with age, while for one born elsewhere (other than Ireland) it is lowest at about 47 years and higher either side.

ann_120.original: Being self-employed in an unincorporated business raises the model's predicted chance of earning at most 50k, through a two-node chain (node 8292, then node 5559) on that workclass level. In the workclass sweep of the typical case, node 5559 is 1.49 for self-employed, not incorporated and 0 for a private employee; the predicted chance moves from 72% (private) to 83%. On the training rows the chain is on for 3034 rows, all of them in that workclass: 0 rows outside it have the chain on, and 3034 training rows are in the workclass. There it adds 0.65 to the score on average. With the step, the mean predicted chance in this workclass is 74.0% against an observed outcome rate of 73.0%; the step raises the mean predicted chance of these 3034 rows by 0.074, so without it the model would rate them as better paid than they are, given their other inputs. Switching the part off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9111.
ann_120.proposed: Self-employment in an unincorporated business raises the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less): a typical person in that work class has about 83% rather than about 72%.

ann_121.original: Shorter working weeks raise the model's predicted chance of earning at most 50k; past a knot near 50 hours this hinge (node 2451) is off and more hours do not move the prediction. In the typical case the predicted chance is 95% at 1 hours, 76% at 36 hours and 60% at 50 hours, and stays at 60% up to 99 hours. The knot lies between 49 hours (node value 0.059) and 50 hours (node value 0). The hinge is on for 31364 training rows (80.3% of them), where it adds 0.70 to the score on average. Switching it off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9076, the second-largest loss among the parts.
ann_121.proposed: Shorter working weeks raise the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less): through this part, more hours lower it steadily up to about 50 hours, then no further.

ann_122.original: Three small units, each switched on by one rare category, each moving the score by a large fixed step for a few people. Node 3389 fires for people born in Trinidad and Tobago (22 training rows with the node on; 22 are Trinidad-born, outcome rate 95.5%): in the typical case the part adds 1.87 to the score and the predicted chance of earning at most 50k is 96%, against 72% for US-born; on the Trinidad-born rows the part raises the mean predicted chance by 0.084, to 95.6%, close to their outcome rate. Node 16072 fires for preschool education (64 rows with the node on; 64 have that education, outcome rate 98.4%): the part adds 1.44 and the predicted chance is 91%; on the actual preschool rows, already predicted near certain, the part raises the mean predicted chance by 0.008 only, to 99.4%, slightly above their outcome rate. Node 1624 fires for people born in Yugoslavia (21 rows, outcome rate 66.7%), where the part adds -1.23 and the predicted chance falls to 51% (on the Yugoslavia-born rows it changes the mean predicted chance by -0.156, to 65.7%), and weakly for state-government workers (node value 0.14 in the typical case against 34.9 for Yugoslavia); it is on for 1616 training rows. The three large steps are fitted to the 22, 64 and 21 rows above. Switching the part off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9117.
ann_122.proposed: A few rare categories each move the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) by a fixed step: birth in Trinidad and Tobago and preschool education raise it, and birth in Yugoslavia lowers it.

ann_123.original: Two units that are on for every training row (100% of the 39073 rows), so each acts as one more linear term on a one-hot input. Node 3843 rises for people listed as an other relative in the household and raises the model's predicted chance of earning at most 50k: in the typical case the node goes from 1.64 (husband) to 4.76 and the part's contribution from -0.03 to 0.92; 1180 training rows have that relationship (outcome rate 96.5%). Node 7420 falls for some-college education and, through its small negative output weight, raises the score slightly: from high-school graduate to some college the node goes from 1.54 to 1.09 and the part's contribution from -0.033 to -0.016. Switching the part to its training mean changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9117.
ann_123.proposed: Living with other relatives raises the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less): a typical person who does has about 87% rather than about 72%; some college barely moves it.

ann_124.original: The direct edges from the inputs to the output, a linear score on the z-scored inputs that carries most of the model's ranking: switching this part to its mean changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.6464. The largest direct terms, on the score per sd of each input, are capital gain -2.52, married to an armed-forces spouse -1.62, married to a civilian spouse -1.43, age -1.03, years of education -0.99, capital loss -0.28 and male sex -0.24; each lowers the predicted chance of earning at most 50k. The never-worked level has a positive term (0.45). Capital gain and age also act through hinges (the capital_gain and age_hinge parts), so their whole-model effect differs from these edge weights; marital status, years of education and sex act through these edges alone in this model. In the typical case, a never-married rather than a civilian-married man has a predicted chance of 98% rather than 72%; an education-num of 13 on the 1-16 scale rather than 9 on the 1-16 scale lowers it from 72% to 35%; a woman rather than a man raises it from 72% to 81%. Because the inputs are z-scored, a rare one-hot level takes a very large value when set, so a moderate weight becomes an extreme score. Married to an armed-forces spouse gives a score of -55.7 in the typical case (predicted chance below 1%); on the 29 training rows with that status the mean predicted chance is below 1% while the outcome rate is 55.2%, a large misfit fitted to few rows. Never worked gives a score of 30.6 (9 training rows, outcome rate 100%). The remaining terms, on occupation, education level, relationship, race, workclass, fnlwgt and many native-country levels, are smaller; the full sum is attached as the formula evidence.
ann_124.proposed: Each input adds its own amount to the score: marriage to a member of the armed forces lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less), older age, capital gains and capital losses lower it steadily, a higher education level lowers it in an uneven way, and being a woman or not being married to a civilian spouse raises it.

ann_125.original: The two capital-gain hinges add on the score, on top of the direct capital-gain edge (-2.52 per sd): above roughly 5000 US dollars each hinge steepens the fall of the model's predicted chance of earning at most 50k, so a large gain is close to decisive. In the typical case the predicted chance is 72% with no gain, 31% at 5000 US dollars and 2% at 10000 US dollars. The two hinges have different exceptions, so they switch separately: at a gain of 20000 US dollars, a US-born typical case has both on (node 1485 at 0.49, node 262 at 1.22, score -10.42); Ecuador-born has node 1485 at 0 with node 262 on (score -7.70); Jamaica-born has node 262 at 0 with node 1485 on (score -7.81). Switching both hinges off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9107.
ann_125.proposed: Large capital gains push the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) further down: through this part, gains change nothing until about 4883 US dollars, then lower it steadily.

ann_126.original: The whole model: the predicted chance of earning at most 50k is the sigmoid of a score, and the score is a constant plus the contributions of the parts, each of which feeds the output node directly, so the parts add on the score. The direct linear terms carry most of the ranking; on top of them the model bends three inputs: age (the predicted chance falls up to 46 years and rises after), hours per week (shorter weeks raise it, with a knot near 50 hours) and capital gain (two hinges above roughly 5000 US dollars make a large gain close to decisive), plus a step for unincorporated self-employment and small steps on a few rare categories. Self-probe of additivity, typical case: moving hours per week from 30 hours to 60 hours changes the score from 1.958 to 0.941 at 30 years and from 1.173 to 0.156 at 60 years, equal steps on the score, while the predicted chance moves from 88% to 72% and from 76% to 54%. Training AUC is 0.9118; with the hidden units that feed the output fixed at their baselines it is 0.8914. Part ablations: direct terms to 0.6464, age hinge to 0.9023, hours hinge to 0.9076, capital gain to 0.9107.
ann_126.proposed: The model adds up seven parts on one score: a direct effect of each input, extra bends for large capital gains, age past the mid-forties and shorter working weeks, and steps for unincorporated self-employment, living with other relatives and a few rare categories. For a typical person, marriage to a member of the armed forces and a professional school degree lower the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less), and being a woman or not being married to a civilian spouse raises it.

parts.name: income_model
parts.original_hypothesis: The whole model: the predicted chance of earning at most 50k is the sigmoid of a score, and the score is a constant plus the contributions of the parts, each of which feeds the output node directly, so the parts add on the score. The direct linear terms carry most of the ranking; on top of them the model bends three inputs: age (the predicted chance falls up to 46 years and rises after), hours per week (shorter weeks raise it, with a knot near 50 hours) and capital gain (two hinges above roughly 5000 US dollars make a large gain close to decisive), plus a step for unincorporated self-employment and small steps on a few rare categories. Self-probe of additivity, typical case: moving hours per week from 30 hours to 60 hours changes the score from 1.958 to 0.941 at 30 years and from 1.173 to 0.156 at 60 years, equal steps on the score, while the predicted chance moves from 88% to 72% and from 76% to 54%. Training AUC is 0.9118; with the hidden units that feed the output fixed at their baselines it is 0.8914. Part ablations: direct terms to 0.6464, age hinge to 0.9023, hours hinge to 0.9076, capital gain to 0.9107.

parts.name: direct_linear_terms
parts.original_hypothesis: The direct edges from the inputs to the output, a linear score on the z-scored inputs that carries most of the model's ranking: switching this part to its mean changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.6464. The largest direct terms, on the score per sd of each input, are capital gain -2.52, married to an armed-forces spouse -1.62, married to a civilian spouse -1.43, age -1.03, years of education -0.99, capital loss -0.28 and male sex -0.24; each lowers the predicted chance of earning at most 50k. The never-worked level has a positive term (0.45). Capital gain and age also act through hinges (the capital_gain and age_hinge parts), so their whole-model effect differs from these edge weights; marital status, years of education and sex act through these edges alone in this model. In the typical case, a never-married rather than a civilian-married man has a predicted chance of 98% rather than 72%; an education-num of 13 on the 1-16 scale rather than 9 on the 1-16 scale lowers it from 72% to 35%; a woman rather than a man raises it from 72% to 81%. Because the inputs are z-scored, a rare one-hot level takes a very large value when set, so a moderate weight becomes an extreme score. Married to an armed-forces spouse gives a score of -55.7 in the typical case (predicted chance below 1%); on the 29 training rows with that status the mean predicted chance is below 1% while the outcome rate is 55.2%, a large misfit fitted to few rows. Never worked gives a score of 30.6 (9 training rows, outcome rate 100%). The remaining terms, on occupation, education level, relationship, race, workclass, fnlwgt and many native-country levels, are smaller; the full sum is attached as the formula evidence.

parts.name: capital_gain
parts.original_hypothesis: The two capital-gain hinges add on the score, on top of the direct capital-gain edge (-2.52 per sd): above roughly 5000 US dollars each hinge steepens the fall of the model's predicted chance of earning at most 50k, so a large gain is close to decisive. In the typical case the predicted chance is 72% with no gain, 31% at 5000 US dollars and 2% at 10000 US dollars. The two hinges have different exceptions, so they switch separately: at a gain of 20000 US dollars, a US-born typical case has both on (node 1485 at 0.49, node 262 at 1.22, score -10.42); Ecuador-born has node 1485 at 0 with node 262 on (score -7.70); Jamaica-born has node 262 at 0 with node 1485 on (score -7.81). Switching both hinges off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9107.

parts.name: capital_gain_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: Through this part, a capital gain above roughly 5200 US dollars pushes the model's predicted chance of earning at most 50k down faster than the direct capital-gain edge does on its own: the model reads a large gain as strong evidence of a higher income. In the typical case (a 37-year-old married man, high-school graduate, 40 hours a week, born in the United States) the hinge node 1485 is off at 5100 US dollars and on at 5200 US dollars, and reaches 0.49 at 20000 US dollars. Its second exit, node 4262, passes the hinge on to the output with a further negative weight, so both exits lower the score as the gain grows. The hinge is on for 1877 training rows, whose outcome rate is 5.8% and mean predicted chance 8%; on those rows the part adds -2.37 to the score on average, against the part's training mean. Birth in Ecuador holds the hinge off: with the Ecuador input set, node 1485 is 0 even at 99999 US dollars. This exception is fitted to few rows: 37 training rows are Ecuador-born and 1 of them has a gain above 5000 dollars. The native-country:15 input of node 4262 has 0 training rows, so its term is constant on the training data. Switching the part off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9114, because the direct capital-gain edge already ranks these rows.

parts.name: age_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: The model's predicted chance of earning at most 50k falls with age up to the mid-forties and rises again after that, as in a career that peaks in mid-life. The fall comes from the direct age edge (-1.03 on the score per sd of age); this part is the rise: a hinge on age (node 2990, then node 5070) whose positive weight more than cancels the direct slope once it is on. In the typical case the predicted chance falls from 92% at 17 years to 56% at 46 years; node 5070 is off at 46 years and on at 47 years (0.096), and the chance climbs back to 67% at 60.8 years and 83% at 90 years. The hinge is on for 10779 training rows, where the part adds 1.10 to the score on average. Birth in Thailand (26 training rows; node 2134 is on for 26 of them and for 26 training rows in total) sets node 2134 to 32.4, which switches the hinge on at each age in the sweep: for a Thai-born typical case the predicted chance rises with age throughout, from 71% at 17 years to 96% at 90 years. This is fitted to 26 rows. Birth in Ireland pushes node 2134 further below its threshold. Switching the part off changes training AUC from 0.9118 to 0.9023.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

ann_117.text: A higher capital gains slightly lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less), and even more so if country of birth is something other than the Netherlands, Ecuador (slowly at first, then faster for people with country of birth other than the Netherlands, Ecuador): for a typical person, capital gains going from 0 US dollars to 6849 US dollars moves the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 72% to about 12% if country of birth is something other than the Netherlands, Ecuador, and from about 78% to about 21% if the country of birth is Ecuador.

Through this part, the model treats a higher capital gains as clearly lowering the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) with nothing until about 5258 US dollars, then steadily: for a typical person, it goes from about 72% at 0 US dollars to about 66% at 6849 US dollars.

Through this part, for a typical person, the model gives a slightly higher predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) if the country of birth is Ecuador (about 72%) than if country of birth is something other than the Netherlands, Ecuador (about 72%).

ann_118.text: This part acts on 1993 of 39073 training people (5%).
For a typical person it acts on, it slightly lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 1% without this part to about 1% with it.
In the training data, 234 of these 1993 people had a low income ($50,000 or less).

Through this part, the model treats a higher capital gains as clearly lowering the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) with nothing until about 4883 US dollars, then steadily: for a typical person, it goes from about 72% at 0 US dollars to about 65% at 6849 US dollars.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: capital gains depending on country of birth lowers it slowly at first, then faster; 9th grade (rather than any other highest education) raises it; Jamaica (rather than any other country of birth) raises it; Nicaragua (rather than any other country of birth) raises it; the Philippines (rather than any other country of birth) raises it; Scotland (rather than any other country of birth) raises it. The model has little data on some of these: only 16 training people (Scotland).

ann_119.text: This part acts on 10779 of 39073 training people (28%).
For a typical person it acts on, it clearly raises the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 33% without this part to about 55% with it.
In the training data, 7116 of these 10779 people had a low income ($50,000 or less).

A higher age clearly lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) if country of birth is something other than Ireland, Thailand, but the other way if the country of birth is Thailand (in a curve that is lowest at about 47 years, higher either side for people with country of birth other than Ireland, Thailand): for a typical person, age going from 22 years to 58 years moves the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 89% to about 65% if country of birth is something other than Ireland, Thailand, and from about 74% to about 90% if the country of birth is Thailand.

Through this part, age clearly adds to the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) once it rises above about 46 years (for 26 of the 39073 training people it already changes below that): for a typical such person, going from 17 years to 63 years moves it from about 72% to about 94%.

Through this part, the model treats a higher age as clearly raising the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) with nothing until about 46 years, then steadily: for a typical person, it goes from about 72% at 22 years to about 90% at 58 years, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher.
